A.explanation: A non-zero needle gives the same zero offset to every potential difference reading, which is a systematic error, so resetting it to zero removes it.

B.explanation: Measuring wire diameter at several points and orientations and averaging reduces random variation from non-uniformity, not a constant systematic shift.

C.explanation: Measuring 100 paperclips reduces the fractional random uncertainty in the mass of one paperclip, but does not remove a constant balance zero error.

D.explanation: Timing 20 oscillations reduces random reaction-time uncertainty in the period of one oscillation, but does not remove a constant systematic timing offset.

hints: Look at what the voltmeter needle not starting at zero would do to every potential difference reading you take.
Recall that a systematic error shifts all readings in the same direction by a fixed amount, while random errors scatter readings above and below.
Compare zeroing the meter with repeating at different wire orientations, using 100 paperclips, or timing 20 oscillations, which all average out scatter and fractional uncertainty.
walkthrough: Identify the error types: systematic error is a repeatable offset in one direction, such as zero error, while random error causes scatter that can be reduced by averaging.
Check option A: if the voltmeter needle does not point to zero with no input, every potential difference measurement will be too high or too low by the same amount.
Adjusting the pointer to the zero position before measuring removes this constant offset, so it directly reduces systematic error.
Check the others: measuring diameter at several orientations, mass of 100 paperclips, and time for 20 oscillations all take a larger total and divide or average.
Those three methods reduce random uncertainty and the percentage effect of reading and reaction-time errors, but they do not remove a fixed zero or calibration shift.
Therefore only zeroing the voltmeter tackles systematic error. This is option A
